subject: science
name: Exploring Magnets
summary: Magnets attract materials like iron, nickel and cobalt (magnetic materials) but not wood, plastic or rubber (non-magnetic materials). Every magnet has a north and a south pole where attraction is strongest. A freely suspended magnet always comes to rest pointing north–south, which is how a compass works. Like poles repel and unlike poles attract. Magnets have many uses and must be handled and stored carefully.

topics.title: Magnets and magnetic materials
topics.summary: A magnet attracts magnetic materials such as iron, nickel and cobalt; materials it does not attract, like wood, plastic and glass, are non-magnetic.
topics.simple: A **magnet** pulls certain things towards itself. Things made of **iron**, **nickel** or **cobalt** are pulled — these are **magnetic materials**. Things like wood, plastic, paper, rubber and glass are not pulled — they are **non-magnetic materials**.
topics.explain:
According to a popular story, long ago a shepherd named **Magnes** in ancient Greece found that the iron tip of his stick and the nails of his shoes stuck to a certain rock. That rock was **magnetite**, a **natural magnet**. Today we mostly use **artificial magnets** made in factories, in shapes such as:
- Bar magnet
- Horseshoe (U-shaped) magnet
- Ring magnet
- Cylindrical and button (disc) magnets

**Magnetic materials** are attracted by a magnet: **iron, nickel, cobalt** and things containing them, such as **steel** (which is mostly iron). Iron nails, pins, steel spoons and paper clips are attracted.

**Non-magnetic materials** are not attracted: wood, plastic, rubber, paper, cloth, glass, leather, and also many metals such as **aluminium, copper, gold and silver**. So not every metal is magnetic!

A magnet can also attract magnetic objects **through** non-magnetic materials like paper, cardboard, wood, glass or water. That's how a magnet can move a pin on top of a sheet of paper from below.
topics.example: If you spill pins on the floor, you can sweep a magnet over the area to collect them. It will pick up the steel pins but leave behind bits of paper, plastic and aluminium foil.
keyPoints: Magnetite is a natural magnet
Artificial magnets: bar, horseshoe, ring, cylindrical, button
Magnetic materials: iron, nickel, cobalt (and steel)
Non-magnetic: wood, plastic, rubber, glass, paper
Not all metals are magnetic: aluminium, copper, gold aren't
Magnets can attract through paper, glass, water

topics.title: Poles of a magnet
topics.summary: The attracting power of a magnet is strongest at its two ends, called poles: the north pole and the south pole. Every magnet has both, even when broken.
topics.simple: Roll a bar magnet in iron filings and you'll see most filings stick at the **two ends**. These ends are called the **poles**, where the magnet is strongest. One is the **north pole** and the other is the **south pole**. Every magnet always has both.
topics.explain:
If you spread **iron filings** on paper and roll a bar magnet in them, the filings gather mostly near the **two ends**, and very few stick to the middle. The places where the attraction is strongest are called the **poles** of the magnet.

- Every magnet has **two poles**: a **north pole (N)** and a **south pole (S)**
- Poles always come in **pairs**. If you break a bar magnet into two pieces, each piece becomes a complete magnet with its own north and south pole. You can never get a magnet with just one pole.
- The poles of a horseshoe magnet are at its two open ends; a ring or disc magnet has its poles on its two flat faces.

The pole that points towards the geographic north when the magnet hangs freely is called the **north-seeking pole** or simply the **north pole**. The other is the south pole.
topics.example: Dip a horseshoe magnet into a box of steel pins: pins cling in a bunch at the two tips of the U, but hardly any stick to the curved middle.
keyPoints: Poles = ends of a magnet where attraction is strongest
Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole
Iron filings collect mostly at the poles
Poles always exist in pairs
A broken magnet gives two complete magnets

topics.title: Finding directions: magnets and the compass
topics.summary: A freely suspended bar magnet always comes to rest along the north–south direction. A compass uses a small magnetised needle to show direction, and you can make one by magnetising a needle.
topics.simple: If you hang a bar magnet from a thread so it can turn freely, it always stops pointing **north and south**. A **compass** uses a tiny magnet (needle) to show directions. You can even make your own compass with a needle, a magnet, a cork and a bowl of water.
topics.explain:
Tie a thread around the middle of a bar magnet and hang it so it can turn freely (away from iron objects). Whichever way you start it, it always comes to rest pointing in the **north–south direction**. The end pointing north is the north pole.

This happens because the **Earth itself behaves like a huge magnet**. Travellers and sailors have used this property for hundreds of years to find directions.

**The compass** is a small box with a magnetised needle that can turn freely on a pivot. The needle's north end is usually painted red. To use it, place it flat and turn the box until the needle lines up with the N–S marks on the dial.

**Making your own compass:**
1. Take an iron needle and a bar magnet
2. Place one pole of the magnet at one end of the needle and **stroke along the needle to the other end**
3. Lift the magnet away, bring it back to the **same starting end** and repeat about 30–40 times, always in the **same direction** with the **same pole**
4. The needle becomes a magnet (check: it now picks up a pin)
5. Push it through a small piece of cork or place it on a leaf, and float it in a bowl of water. It turns to point north–south.
topics.example: Fishermen, trekkers and soldiers use compasses where there are no landmarks, such as at sea or in thick forests. Many mobile phones also have a digital compass inside.
keyPoints: A freely suspended magnet rests in the north–south direction
Earth behaves like a giant magnet
A compass has a freely turning magnetised needle
Magnetise a needle by stroking it 30–40 times in one direction with one pole
A magnetised needle on cork floating in water acts as a compass
Keep iron objects away when using a compass

topics.title: Attraction and repulsion
topics.summary: Unlike poles (N and S) attract each other; like poles (N–N or S–S) repel. Repulsion is the sure test of whether an object is a magnet.
topics.simple: Bring two magnets close. If a **north pole** faces a **south pole**, they pull together (**attract**). If two north poles or two south poles face each other, they push apart (**repel**). Opposites attract, likes repel.
topics.explain:
When two magnets are brought near each other:
- **Unlike poles attract:** N and S pull towards each other
- **Like poles repel:** N and N, or S and S, push each other away

You can feel the push of repulsion if you try to force two like poles together. Placing two ring magnets with like poles facing on a pencil makes the top one **float** in the air!

**How do you know if something is a magnet?**
- **Attraction is not enough:** a magnet attracts a plain iron bar, and an iron bar is attracted to a magnet, from either end. So attraction can't tell you which one is the magnet.
- **Repulsion is the sure test:** only a magnet can repel another magnet. If one end of an object pushes away a pole of a known magnet, the object must be a magnet.

**Finding an unknown pole:** bring the known north pole of a magnet near the end of another magnet. If they repel, that end is also a north pole; if they attract, it is a south pole.
topics.example: Two toy cars with bar magnets fixed on them: if the facing ends are N and S, one car pulls the other; if the facing ends are both N, one car pushes the other away without touching it.
keyPoints: Unlike poles attract (N–S)
Like poles repel (N–N, S–S)
Repulsion is the sure test of a magnet
Iron is attracted by both poles, so attraction alone doesn't prove magnetism
Use a known pole to identify an unknown pole

topics.title: Uses of magnets and how to take care of them
topics.summary: Magnets are used in compasses, fridge doors, toys, pencil boxes, speakers and cranes; they lose magnetism if heated, hammered or dropped, so they are stored with keepers or in pairs with unlike poles together.
topics.simple: Magnets are used in many things: refrigerator doors, pencil boxes, toys, speakers, compasses and big cranes that lift scrap iron. Magnets can become weak if you **heat**, **hammer** or **drop** them, so keep them carefully and away from phones and computers.
topics.explain:
**Uses of magnets**
- Compass for finding direction
- Refrigerator doors and magnetic pencil boxes (keep them shut)
- Fridge magnets, magnetic toys and games
- Speakers, earphones and some electric motors
- Large **electromagnet cranes** to lift and separate iron scrap
- Separating iron pieces from waste or from grain
- Mechanics use magnetised screwdrivers so screws don't fall

**Magnets lose their magnetism if they are:**
- Heated
- Hammered
- Dropped from a height again and again

**Storing magnets properly**
- Keep **bar magnets in pairs** with **unlike poles on the same side** (N next to S), separated by a piece of wood, with two pieces of **soft iron (keepers)** placed across their ends
- Keep a **horseshoe magnet** with a keeper (iron piece) across its poles
- Keep magnets **away from** mobile phones, computers, TVs, music systems, credit/debit cards and CDs, because magnets can damage them
topics.example: In a scrapyard, a big crane with a powerful magnet picks up a pile of iron and steel junk, leaving plastic and wood behind, and drops it elsewhere when the magnet is switched off.
keyPoints: Uses: compass, fridge doors, pencil boxes, speakers, toys, cranes
Heating, hammering or dropping weakens a magnet
Store bar magnets in pairs, unlike poles together, with keepers
Horseshoe magnet: keep a keeper across its poles
Keep magnets away from phones, computers, cards

keyConcepts.meaning: An object that attracts iron, nickel and cobalt and has a north and a south pole.
A natural rock that behaves like a magnet.

The pole of a freely suspended magnet that points towards the north.

Pulling together — happens between unlike poles, and between a magnet and a magnetic material.
Pushing apart — happens only between like poles of two magnets.
A piece of soft iron placed across the poles of stored magnets to help them keep their magnetism.

commonMistakes: Thinking all metals are magnetic — aluminium, copper, gold and silver are not.
Using attraction to prove something is a magnet — repulsion is the only sure test.
Thinking a broken magnet has only one pole in each piece — each piece gets both N and S.
Stroking the needle back and forth when making a magnet — always stroke in one direction with the same pole.
Storing bar magnets with like poles together — store with unlike poles side by side and keepers at the ends.
Thinking the middle of a bar magnet is the strongest part — the poles are.

faqs.q: Why is repulsion, and not attraction, the sure test of a magnet?
faqs.a: A magnet attracts an ordinary iron object too, so if two objects attract, one of them might just be iron. But **repulsion only happens between two magnets** (like poles). So if an object repels a pole of a magnet, it must be a magnet.
No. Only iron, nickel, cobalt and materials containing them (like steel) are magnetic. Metals such as aluminium, copper, brass, gold and silver are not attracted by a magnet.

faqs.q: What happens if you break a bar magnet into two?
faqs.a: Each piece becomes a complete, smaller magnet with its own north and south pole. You can't get a magnet with only one pole.

faqs.q: How can I find which end of a magnet is north if it isn't marked?
faqs.a: Hang it freely from a thread. The end that points north is its north pole. Or bring it near the marked north pole of another magnet: if they **repel**, it's a north pole; if they **attract**, it's a south pole.

quiz.q: Which of these is a magnetic material?
quiz.explain: Iron is attracted by a magnet; copper and aluminium are non-magnetic metals.
Magnetite is a rock that naturally behaves like a magnet.

quiz.q: A freely suspended bar magnet always comes to rest pointing:
quiz.explain: This property is used in a compass.

quiz.q: To magnetise an iron needle with a bar magnet, you should stroke it:
options: From one end to the other in the same direction, using the same pole
quiz.explain: Stroking repeatedly in one direction with one pole turns the needle into a magnet.

Which is the sure test to find out whether an iron bar is a magnet?
options: It repels one pole of a known magnet
quiz.explain: Only a magnet can repel another magnet; plain iron is attracted by both poles.

quiz.q: End X of a magnet attracts the north pole of a compass needle. End X is a:
quiz.explain: Unlike poles attract, so X must be a south pole.

quiz.q: Which of these can make a magnet lose its magnetism?
options: Storing it in a wooden box
quiz.explain: Heating, hammering and repeated dropping weaken magnets.

quiz.q: The correct way to store two bar magnets is:
options: Thrown loosely in a drawer with keys
Unlike poles on the same side, separated by wood, with soft iron keepers at the ends
quiz.explain: Pairs with unlike poles together and keepers help magnets keep their strength.

quiz.q: A magnet held under a sheet of paper can still move a pin on top of it. This shows that:
options: A magnet can attract through non-magnetic materials
